records.name: The Bosporus at Constantinople

tide.phaseNote: No usable tide (the Black Sea and Marmara tides are a few cm). The water runs one way all day: the Black Sea end stands about 40 cm above the Marmara end, so the surface current sets south, 3-4 kn as a rule, up to 7 kn when north winds blow over the Black Sea, 7-8 kn at the Kandilli-Asiyan narrows.
tide.notes: The 'tide' a sailor meets here is the current and the wind on it. Strong south winds (lodos, kible) can push the surface water north over the whole strait for a time; in the bays the water runs back north as counter-currents (anafor), with whirls ('ayna') where they rejoin the main stream (tr.wikipedia).

waves.swellFrom: N/NE: Black Sea swell runs into the north mouth in NE gales; S/SW: Marmara sea (lodos) at the south mouth by the city
waves.notes: Inside the strait the sea is short chop on a fast current (estimate from fetches of 2-15 km between the bends). Wind against the current (a S wind on the S-going stream) gives steep breaking chop off the points (estimate). No wave record was found for the strait; all wave values are estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Two-layer exchange: the fresher upper layer runs Black Sea to Marmara at 1.5-2 m/s, the salty lower layer runs north at 0.9-1 m/s (ru.wikipedia); the lower current starts 15-20 m down and fills to about 45 m (tr.wikipedia), interface about 40 m (de.wikipedia); about 16,000 m3/s out on top and 11,000 m3/s in below (en.wikipedia). Strongest from Kandilli southward and at Arnavutkoy point.
sea.seaIceOneIn: Very rare: floating ice from the Black Sea passed Constantinople in the winter of 763/764, thirty years before the game starts (Theophanes, via en.wikipedia '764'). (guess) once in 150-300 years; the decision-17 cooling of 793-900 raises the odds a little.
sea.notes: Length 31 km, width 700 m (Kandilli-Asiyan) to 3,420 m; depth 13-110 m in midstream, average 65 m (en.wikipedia; de.wikipedia gives 124 m off Bebek). A 45-degree turn at Kandilli and an 80-degree turn at Yenikoy (en.wikipedia).

optics.colour: Dark blue-green out in the stream, cobalt in sun, bottle-green over the shallow edges; the surface water is Black Sea water and carries its plankton colour; foam lines and slicks mark the current seams.
optics.turbidityCause: Plankton in the Black Sea outflow (spring and early-summer blooms); streams and street runoff after winter rain near the city

salinityPsu.note: Surface 17-18 at the north end (Black Sea), rising toward Marmara (whose surface is about 22, en.wikipedia Sea of Marmara); lower layer 35-38 (Marmara/Mediterranean water). Bosporus water is saltiest in November, freshest in June (tr.wikipedia). Secchi and temperatures are estimates.

hazards.name: Kandilli-Asiyan narrows
hazards.where: The 700 m narrows between Kandilli and Asiyan (by Bebek)
hazards.danger: 7-8 kn current with a 45-degree turn; a ship under oar cannot stem it and must track along the bank or use a counter-current (estimate)

hazards.name: Arnavutkoy point (Akintiburnu, 'current point')
hazards.danger: Fastest surface current; whirls where the counter-currents meet the stream

hazards.name: Yenikoy bend
hazards.where: European shore, middle of the strait
hazards.danger: 80-degree turn in the current

hazards.name: Bay counter-currents
hazards.where: The bays at Beylerbeyi, Vanikoy, Anadoluhisari and Istinye
hazards.danger: Back-eddies swing a ship round; also the way to make northing against the stream

phenomena: hard current seams with foam lines and slicks off every point
back-eddies and whirls in the bays
steep standing chop where the wind opposes the current
spring sea fog (estimate: March-May)

records.change_800_to_1066: No physical change of note. The Medieval Climate Anomaly after about 950 makes the winters a little milder (decision 17).
records.then_vs_now: The exchange flow is natural and the same as now. The shores were natural rock, beach and wooden landings, with no modern quays or fill. The Black Sea rivers were not dammed, so the fresh surplus and the spring outflow were a little larger (estimate). The sea stood perhaps 0.5-1 m lower (guess; see black_sea_open).

records.name: The open Black Sea (Pontos Euxeinos)

tide.phaseNote: Tides so small they show only on instruments (ru.wikipedia). Treat as no tide; the ranges are estimates.
tide.notes: Seiches in bays reach 40-50 cm with periods from minutes to hours (ru.wikipedia): the only quick level change a sailor sees.

waves.swellFrom: Winter: NE (prevailing, 7-8 m/s) and SW storms; autumn storms worst in the NE; summer: light NW
waves.notes: Hindcast 1949-2010 (Arkhipkin et al. 2014): mean Hs under 0.7 m; winter mean over 0.95 m in the centre; maximum Hs over 6.5 m with wavelength over 55 m and period over 7 s in winter and autumn; 6.52 m, 58.6 m and 7.4 s on 11 Nov 2007; storms with Hs over 5 m only October-March, the longest in February; 100-year Hs over 14 m off south-west, south and south-east Crimea; at least 5.8 m measured in the Bulgarian storm of February 1979. The paper's seasonal mean periods (2.4-2.5 s) are a model mean period; TpMeanS 4.5 is an estimate of the peak period. Hs99 is an estimate. The Fetch table is from the basin's size (1,175 km east-west, en.wikipedia), rough.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: The Rim Current runs anticlockwise round the basin at up to 0.5-1.0 m/s (en.wikipedia), with eddies inside it: south along Bulgaria, east along Anatolia, north along Georgia, west along the Caucasus and Crimea.
sea.seaIceOneIn: Open sea: never. Shore-fast ice on the north coast only in very hard, long winters, not more than once in several decades (ru.wikipedia); the north-west shelf bays and the limans freeze more often (see dnieper_bug_liman_berezan). The great freeze of 763/764 sent floes past Constantinople (en.wikipedia '764').
sea.notes: Area 436,400 km2, 1,175 km east-west, mean depth 1,253 m, maximum 2,212 m (en.wikipedia). Steep slopes and a narrow shelf except in the north-west and west (Arkhipkin et al. 2014). Below 150-200 m the water holds hydrogen sulphide; over 90% of the deep volume is anoxic (ru, en.wikipedia). Invisible from a ship; it means no life and perfectly kept wrecks below about 150 m.

optics.colour: Deep blue to inky blue-grey; under overcast and in winter storms nearly black-green, which is how it looks to a northern sailor; milky turquoise patches in early summer when coccolithophore blooms whiten it (knowledge).
optics.turbidityCause: Plankton (spring diatoms, early-summer coccolithophores, late-summer dinoflagellates); river plumes only on the north-west shelf

salinityPsu.note: Surface about 17-18, deep 22-22.5 (ru, en.wikipedia): half of ocean salinity. Secchi values are pre-eutrophication guesses (knowledge, not re-verified).

hazards.where: South-west in winter, north-east in autumn
hazards.danger: Hs over 6.5 m (hindcast); a 100-year sea over 14 m south of Crimea

hazards.danger: Down-slope wind 25-30 m/s on the coast (Arkhipkin et al. 2014)

records.then_vs_now: Before the 1960s-80s eutrophication from the Danube and Dnieper the open sea was clearer: summer Secchi 15-20 m (guess from pre-eutrophication literature, not re-verified). No comb-jelly invasion (Mnemiopsis came in the 1980s, knowledge). Sea level about 0.5-1 m lower than now (guess: the Tuzla page gives 4 m lower 2,500 years ago, and a third of Phanagoria now lies under the sea).

records.name: The Danube delta: the St George (Sfântu Gheorghe) branch at Preslavets
levels: The Bulgar coast and the Danube

tide.phaseNote: No tide (the Black Sea tide is instrument-only). The river's level follows the seasons and wind set-up at the mouth.
tide.tidalLimit: none
tide.notes: At the mouth a bar of river sand; onshore gales back the water up the branch (estimate).

river.name: Danube, St George branch
river.floodMonths: April-June (Alpine and Carpathian snowmelt); a lesser rise with autumn rain
features: reed marsh and lakes behind the levees
a sand bar at the mouth
river.notes: The St George is the oldest branch; its lobe (St George II) has been building since the turn of the era, while the Chilia lobe that carries most of the water today only began about 1600 AD (en.wikipedia Danube Delta). So c. 800 the St George was the main working mouth: its share of the flow is a guess of 40-60% of the Danube's 6,452 m3/s mean (en.wikipedia Danube, 1931-2020; min 1,790, max 15,900), against 1,500 m3/s today (1921-1990, en.wikipedia Danube Delta). Its length was 108 km before the meander cuts shortened it to 70 km (same). 40% of the delta was built in the last 1,000 years (Giosan, same), so the delta front c. 800 lay several km inland of today's (estimate). Width, depth, current, rise and gradient are estimates. The Danube freezes in part almost every year and forms an ice bridge somewhere in one year of two or three (ro.wikipedia Dunărea); the delta branches closing about one winter in four c. 800 is a guess with the decision-17 cooling.

optics.colour: Opaque olive-brown in summer, khaki-brown in the spring flood; the plume makes a sharp brown-against-green front at the mouth; reed lakes behind the levees are clear and dark.
optics.turbidityCause: Suspended silt (the Danube carries tens of millions of tonnes a year, en.wikipedia), more in flood

salinityPsu.note: Fresh in the branch; the Black Sea's 17-18 only beyond the bar (estimate)

hazards.danger: Floes on the current; damage to moored hulls (estimate)

floating reed islands
drift ice at the thaw
records.change_800_to_1066: The delta front grows seaward (40% of the delta in the last 1,000 years, sediment rising with forest clearance upstream). Preslavets enters the game in 968; Sviatoslav's Danube capital 969-971.
records.then_vs_now: No Iron Gates dams (1972) and no levees: higher sediment and a free floodplain (estimate). The St George was the main mouth, not the Chilia. The St George still had its six big meanders. The Razelm (Halmyris) lagoon south of the delta was more open to the sea than today (guess).

river.notes: Discharge is the mouth's 1931-2020 record (mean 6,452, min 1,790, max 15,900 m3/s, en.wikipedia) less the Siret and Prut, which join below Silistra (estimate). The Lower Danube is about 400 m wide near Braila in its main channel and averages 9 m deep (en.wikipedia); at Silistra the river with its side channels is wider, 800 m is an estimate. Current, flood rise and gradient are estimates. Freezing: partial nearly every year, an ice bridge at some point one year in two or three (ro.wikipedia); the chronicle's winter of 821/822 froze the Danube hard enough for carts for thirty days (ARF 821, via Design/weather_and_sea_state.md 1.2). One winter in five closed at Silistra c. 800 is a guess.

optics.colour: Grey-brown to olive, opaque; bright khaki in the spring flood; clearer and greener in a still winter.
optics.turbidityCause: Silt; reconstructed sediment loads of 52.9-81.7 million tonnes a year (en.wikipedia)

records.then_vs_now: No dams upstream (the Iron Gates came in 1972) and no dykes: the floodplain floods every spring and the river carries more sediment (estimate).

river.name: Dnieper and Southern Bug, through the liman
features: the Kinburn spit and the Ochakiv cape enclosing the 3.6 km strait
the Dnieper delta and its reed marsh (plavni) at the head
river.notes: The liman: the Dnieper part 55 km long and up to 17 km wide, the Bug part 47 km by 5-11 km; depth mostly 6-7 m, up to 12 m; joined to the sea by a 3.6 km strait between the Ochakiv cape and the Kinburn spit (ru, uk.wikipedia). Dnieper mean 1,670-1,700 m3/s at the mouth, 1,370 at Kyiv with 7,000 in spring (ru.wikipedia); low and flood values here are estimates for the undammed river. The liman freezing in most winters c. 800 is an estimate (nearly fresh water, the decision-17 cooling). Berezan is a limestone island 900 x 320 m, 3-6 m high in the north and 21 m in the south, about 2 km from the mainland shore and about 7 km from the liman's mouth (en, ru.wikipedia); the Greeks knew it as a peninsula (uk.wikipedia), so by 800 it was an island, the place where the Rus fitted their monoxyla with masts and sails (knowledge, De Administrando Imperio).

waves.swellFrom: S and SW over the shallow north-west shelf
waves.notes: Shallow shelf limits the sea (estimate; depths 10-20 m round Berezan). All values estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Liman water flows out along the Ochakiv side; wind-driven currents on the shelf (estimate).
sea.seaIceOneIn: The north-west shelf bays freeze in hard winters (en.wikipedia Black Sea shows ice on the Gulf of Odesa); (estimate) the sea round Berezan holds floe ice one winter in 3-4 c. 800.
sea.notes: The Rus came down the Dnieper past the rapids (50 m of fall in 66 km, nine great rapids, drowned by the 1932 dam: en.wikipedia Dnieper Rapids) and out through the liman to Berezan.

optics.colour: Liman: green-brown, opaque; off Berezan the brown river water lies over greener sea water, with a visible edge on calm days.
optics.turbidityCause: Dnieper silt and plankton (a fresh, shallow, warm-summer liman)

salinityPsu.note: Mean 3.6 today, about 2 before the Kakhovka reservoir (uk.wikipedia); with the full undammed flow c. 800 lower still, 0.5-2 (estimate). Off Berezan 5-12 depending on wind and season (estimate).

sea.seaIceOneIn: Azov ice drifts south through the strait into the Black Sea (ru.wikipedia Азовское море); (estimate) floe ice in the strait most winters c. 800, fast ice in the northern narrows one winter in 2-3.
sea.notes: 35-41 km long, 3.1-4.5 km at the narrowest (Chushka spit) to 15 km wide, at most 18 m deep (en, ru.wikipedia). Fog is a known hazard (en.wikipedia Kerch Strait).

records.change_800_to_1066: Tamatarcha becomes Tmutarakan, a Rus principality, about 988-1094 (en.wikipedia Tmutarakan). The water does not change much.
records.then_vs_now: The Tuzla spit was continuous with Taman (cut in 1925). The sea stood lower (4 m lower 2,500 years ago per en.wikipedia Tuzla Island; about 0.5-1 m lower c. 800, guess), so Phanagoria's lower town, now a third under water, was dry or awash. The Taman peninsula had been an archipelago in antiquity (en.wikipedia Phanagoria) and the Kuban delta was still filling it (guess). No modern dredged channel; natural depth only.

records.name: The Sea of Azov (Maeotis)
levels: The Sea of Azov and the Don

tide.phaseNote: No tide; wind set-up, set-down and seiches of 20-50 cm lasting minutes to hours (en.wikipedia).
tide.notes: East winds drain Taganrog Bay and the Don mouth, west winds pile water into them (knowledge: set-up and set-down of 1-3 m at Taganrog, not re-verified). Dried-out shallows after an east wind are the 'flats'.

waves.swellFrom: No swell: short steep wind sea from E/NE (winter) and W/SW
waves.notes: Open-sea waves usually 1-2 m, sometimes 3 m; 2-4 m near the southern shores; 1 m in the Kerch strait (en.wikipedia). The same page gives 6 m in Taganrog Bay, which cannot be a wave height in a bay 4.9 m deep on average (ru.wikipedia Таганрогский залив): treat it as doubtful (perhaps a surge or a crest-to-trough storm wave); a depth-limited Hs of about 2-2.5 m is the estimate for the bay. Short, steep and breaking: the classic Azov chop.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Anticlockwise drift under the westerlies, usually under 10 cm/s, up to 60-70 cm/s in 15-20 m/s winds (en.wikipedia).
sea.seaIceOneIn: Every winter, late December to mid-March; 30-40 cm thick in most of the sea, 60-80 cm in Taganrog Bay; shore-fast bands 7 km wide in the north to 1.5 km in the south; ridges piled several metres high; navigation stopped in winter before icebreakers (en.wikipedia). With the decision-17 cooling c. 800, a full freeze of Taganrog Bay every winter for about 3 months and of the open sea in most winters (estimate).
sea.notes: 39,000 km2, 360 x 180 km, mean depth 7 m, maximum 14 m (13.5-14 now, 16 in older surveys: en.wikipedia). Rivers bring 38.6 km3 a year, the Don about twice the Kuban (same). The Syvash lagoons behind the 112 km Arabat spit are 0.5-1 m deep and salinity 170 (same).

optics.colour: Taganrog Bay greenish-yellow to brownish-yellow (Secchi 0.5-0.9 m, rarely 2 m); the central sea greenish-blue (1.5-2.5 m, up to 8 m); bright green in summer blooms (ru.wikipedia).
optics.turbidityCause: Muddy river water, bottom silt stirred by every blow in a 7 m sea, and dense plankton (ru.wikipedia)

salinityPsu.note: Before 1950s regulation: 1 at the Don mouth, 10.5 in the centre, 11.5 at the Kerch strait (ru.wikipedia); today 10-12 open sea, 2-7 in Taganrog Bay (en.wikipedia)

hazards.name: Ice
hazards.where: Whole sea December-March; worst in Taganrog Bay
hazards.danger: Closed to ships; ridged ice several metres high (en.wikipedia)

hazards.where: The long spits of the north and west shores (Arabat 112 km, Fedotov, Berdyansk, Dolgaya, Belosarayskaya)
hazards.danger: Grounding on long low sand (en.wikipedia)

hazards.where: Taganrog Bay and the Don delta after east winds
hazards.danger: Water drains away and the channel shoals (estimate)

hazards.name: Short steep chop

bright green summer blooms

mud-volcano islands appearing off Taman (rare)
records.change_800_to_1066: Milder winters after about 950. The Don delta front advances seaward (estimate).
records.then_vs_now: No Tsimlyansk dam (1952): the Don's spring flood ran full, so the sea was fresher (1 to 10.5 psu, ru.wikipedia), the fish richer, the flood plume larger. The sea was deeper by the 2 m of silt laid since (16 m in older surveys vs 14 now, en.wikipedia, scaled back to 800 as a guess). Sea level perhaps 0.5-1 m lower (guess).

river.name: Don (Tanais)
river.floodMonths: April-May, often in two waves: first the 'cold' water from the lower basin's snowmelt, then the 'warm' water from the upper Don
river.lowMonths: July-February (slow fall from the end of the flood to the next spring)
features: a floodplain valley 12-15 km wide in the lower course
Sarkel's cape on the left bank cut off by a moat
river.notes: Mean 680 m3/s at Razdorskaya, 900 for the basin as a whole; gradient 0.096 m/km; spring flood with the level swinging 8-13 m along the river; snow gives up to 70% of the water; freezes late November to early December, 30-90 days of ice in the lower course, thaw from late March (ru.wikipedia). Low and flood discharge, width, depth and current are estimates for the undammed river. With the decision-17 cooling, 70-110 days of ice c. 800 (estimate): the river freezes every winter. Sarkel: a brick fort of 193.5 x 133.5 m with walls 3.75 m thick and at least 10 m high, built 834-837 on a cape cut off from the bank by a moat (ru.wikipedia). The haul to the Volga runs from the Don's great bend near Kalach, about 70 km (ru.wikipedia, via the fetch).

records.then_vs_now: Sarkel and the reach now lie under the Tsimlyansk reservoir (1952); below it four locks and weirs keep the depth (ru.wikipedia). c. 800 the Don was free, with its full spring flood and shallow summer riffles.

records.name: The open Caspian (the Khazar Sea)

tide.phaseNote: No tide of any use (a few cm, knowledge). The level is set by the Volga's water against evaporation and moves metres over decades and centuries; day to day only wind set-up and seiche.
tide.notes: LEVEL c. 800 (the big one). The sea level is relative to the ocean. Naderi Beni et al. 2013 weigh the historical and geological evidence: the 10th century is 'the most controversial time period' of the last millennium, put below -35 m (Varushchenko 1987), at -33 m (Gumilev 1980, Karpychev), and above -17 m (Bruckner 1890). They favour about -23 m in 907 (Chalus and Ramsar, where the sea met the mountains), -23.8 m in 982 (Bab island on the map), a fall from 977 (Ibn Hawqal saw the sea shallowing in Dahestan) into the Medieval Climate Anomaly low of about -28 m, Abaskun on the shoreline at about -24 m in 1208, and a rapid rise to -19 m by 1304 that drowned Abaskun. Today: about -27 m in the long record, below -29 m in July 2025 (en.wikipedia); -25.2 m in 1882 and -29.0 m in 1977 (az.wikipedia). WORKING VALUE for the game: -25 m (estimate) for 793-975, falling to -27.5 m by 1000 and -28 m by 1066 (estimate), i.e. 3-4 m above today's sea in the 9th century and about level with it at the end of the game. Doubt: low; the Soviet school's -32 to -36 m would put the 9th-century shore tens of km seaward of today's in the north.

waves.swellFrom: N and NW (dominant); SE in the north half and at Makhachkala-Derbent
waves.notes: The highest wave recorded, 11 m, off the Apsheron peninsula, Makhachkala and Derbent, the windiest places; autumn and winter winds often reach 35-40 m/s (ru.wikipedia). Light NW winds (about 6 m/s) give waves up to 1 m over 75% of the Middle and South Caspian; 16-20 m/s N-NW gales give waves of 3 m and more over about 80% of it, under 2 m only at the far south; at 25 m/s and more the storm waves reach 7.5-7.8 m at their centre, 70-90 km north of Apsheron; a 50-year wave of 17 m is computed for the Neft Daslari area and 15 m for the South Caspian (az.wikipedia; these are individual wave heights, not Hs). The 11 m is an individual wave (HsMaxRecordedM holds it for lack of a recorded Hs). Mean Hs, Hs99 and Tp are estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: A strong current carries North Caspian water south along the west coast to Apsheron, where it splits: one branch on south along the west shore, one across to the east (ru.wikipedia). (estimate) 0.1-0.3 m/s, faster off capes in gales.
sea.seaIceOneIn: The North Caspian freezes every year; in hard winters the west and east coasts of the Middle Caspian ice up in bays (coastal ice at Makhachkala in 72-74% of winters, at Sumgait about 20%); heavy pack drifted to Apsheron in 1928-29, 1949-50, 1953-54, 1968-69 and 1971-72 (az.wikipedia). The south never (estimate).
sea.notes: 1,200 km north-south, 320 km wide on average, 371,000-389,000 km2, mean depth 211 m; the North Caspian 4-8 m deep (5-6 m average, at most 25 m), the Middle 190 m average with the Derbent depression to 788 m, the South over 1,000 m to 1,025 m; the Mangyshlak sill parts north from middle, the Apsheron sill (about 198 m) middle from south (en, ru, az.wikipedia). The Volga brings about 80% of the inflow (en.wikipedia).

optics.colour: Middle and South: clear blue-green to deep blue, Secchi 10-15 m in the centre and up to about 20 m in the South Caspian in summer; the west coast duller and greener than the east; the north turbid grey-green.
optics.turbidityCause: Plankton offshore; the Volga, Terek, Sulak, Samur and Kura plumes along the west coast

salinityPsu.note: Mean 12.8-12.9; from about 0.1 at the Volga and Ural mouths to 10-11 at the North-Middle boundary and 11-13 in the south-east (ru.wikipedia). A 3-4 m higher sea c. 800 means a slightly larger, slightly fresher sea (estimate, small).

hazards.name: North and NW gales
hazards.where: Middle Caspian, worst 70-90 km north of Apsheron

records.name: The North Caspian shallows off the Volga delta

tide.phaseNote: No tide. Wind surges (nagon) and set-downs (sgon) are the 'tides' here: strong ones mainly in autumn and winter, once or twice in spring (az.wikipedia).
tide.notes: On a sea a few metres deep over a nearly flat plain, a SE or E gale can push the water km inland over the delta's front and a NW gale can drain it off the shallows (knowledge: surges of 2-3 m reaching tens of km inland on the flat north coast, not re-verified).

waves.swellFrom: No swell: short depth-limited wind sea from the SE, S and E
waves.notes: Depth-limited: in 4-8 m of water Hs cannot much exceed 2-3 m (estimate, Hs <= 0.5 h); SE winds raise strong winds and seas over the north half (az.wikipedia). All values estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Volga water spreads south and west and runs down the west coast (ru.wikipedia); wind-driven drift dominates (estimate).
sea.seaIceOneIn: Every winter: fast ice over the whole North Caspian (az.wikipedia: 'covered every year by fixed, solid ice'); the seals pup on it in late January-early February (en.wikipedia Caspian seal). Duration and thickness c. 800: December to March, 30-60 cm (knowledge, not re-verified; more in the decision-17 winters).
sea.notes: Average depth 4-8 m, at most 25 m; a gently undulating plain of banks and built-up islands (ru.wikipedia). With the sea at about -25 m c. 800 instead of -29 m today, the shoreline over this plain lay far inland of today's and the Volga delta was much smaller: the delta grew from 3,222 km2 in 1880 to 27,224 km2 now largely as the sea fell (en.wikipedia Volga Delta), and the reverse holds for 800 (estimate).

optics.colour: Grey-green to yellow-grey and cloudy; in April the Volga's melt makes it turbid (Secchi under 2-2.4 m); white ice from December to March.
optics.turbidityCause: Volga silt and bottom mud stirred in a 5 m sea; plankton

salinityPsu.note: 0.1 at the Volga mouths rising to 10-11 at the boundary with the Middle Caspian; freshest in June (ru.wikipedia)

tide.phaseNote: No tide. Caspian wind surges reach up the lower delta channels in autumn (estimate).

river.name: Volga (Itil, Atil)
river.floodMonths: April-June (the natural spring flood carries 60-70% of the year's water); a smaller autumn rain rise in October
features: up to 500 branches, channels and creeks in the delta
main branches Buzan, Bakhtemir, Kamyzyak and the Akhtuba
Baer knolls: sand ridges 5-22 m high (average 8 m), 0.4-10 km long
river.notes: Mean 8,060 m3/s at Volgograd; flood peaks used to reach 67,000 m3/s below the Kama and up to 52,000 at Volgograd, held down by spreading over the floodplain; before regulation the level swung 3 m a year at Astrakhan; at Astrakhan the river opens in mid-March and is ice-free about 260 days, i.e. about 105 days of ice; pre-dam sediment about 25 million tonnes a year; snow 60%, ground water 30%, rain 10% (ru.wikipedia). The delta starts where the Buzan leaves the Volga, 46 km above Astrakhan, and counts up to 500 channels (same). The Akhtuba is 200-300 m wide, in places 50 m (ru.wikipedia). Low and flood discharge at Itil, width, depth, current and gradient are estimates; ice c. 800 about 110-125 days with the decision-17 cooling (estimate). ITIL: three parts on the river, the west (court, garrison), the east (trade, baths, shops) and an island between with the palaces of the khagan and the bek, joined by a pontoon bridge (en.wikipedia Atil, from the Arab geographers). Its site is unknown; the Samosdelka claim is disproved; Semibugry in the central delta is being dug; one view is that the site was washed away by the Caspian's later rises (same).

optics.colour: Opaque yellow-brown in the May-June flood, olive-grey in summer, clearer green-brown in the side channels and ilmens; ice from December to mid-March.
optics.turbidityCause: Silt (25 Mt a year before the dams); plankton in summer backwaters

records.change_800_to_1066: Itil is sacked by Sviatoslav in 968/969 and is in ruins by the 11th century (ru.wikipedia, citing al-Biruni). As the Caspian falls after 977 the delta grows seaward (estimate).
records.then_vs_now: No dams (the Volgograd dam is from 1961): the full natural flood every spring, much less winter flow, more sediment; the Caspian about 3-4 m higher c. 800, so the delta was smaller and its front lay further north, perhaps near today's Astrakhan region (estimate).

records.name: The western shore: Samandar and Bab al-Abwab (Derbent)

tide.phaseNote: No tide; wind set-up and seiche only. The 958 earthquake raised and dropped the sea at Baku by about 0.45 m and flooded part of the Terek delta shore (Naderi Beni et al. 2013, table 6).

waves.swellFrom: SE storms (characteristic of Makhachkala-Derbent), N-NW gales, E
waves.notes: Makhachkala and Derbent are among the windiest places on the Caspian, where the 11 m wave was recorded (ru.wikipedia); SE storms are typical of the Makhachkala-Derbent coast (az.wikipedia). Mean, 99% and Tp are estimates; the fetch table is rough.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: The southward coastal current from the North Caspian runs along this shore to Apsheron (ru.wikipedia); (estimate) 0.1-0.3 m/s.
sea.seaIceOneIn: Coastal ice at Makhachkala in 72-74% of winters today (az.wikipedia); c. 800 nearly every winter (estimate); at Derbent less, one winter in 2-3 (estimate). Drift ice from the north in extreme winters (az.wikipedia).
sea.notes: A straight open coast with a narrow shelf (60-100 m wide zone, az.wikipedia) and the Derbent depression (788 m) offshore. Derbent's Sasanian walls ran down to the sea and out into it to make a harbour; it was the port for ships between Iran and Itil, where goods moved from ships to caravans (en, ru.wikipedia). Al-Mas'udi (947) says the wall ran a mile into the sea, and in 915-921 six of the wall's projections stood in the water (Naderi Beni et al. 2013, tables 3 and 4). The 918 earthquake sank part of the shore with its fortifications, and a shoreline shift of about 150 m is recorded (same, table 6). Samandar's site is unknown (the levels file stands it in near Tarki); the Terek delta lies to the north with water of 400-500 g/m3 silt, twice the Volga's, and ice only in some hard winters (ru.wikipedia Терек).

optics.colour: Green-blue and fairly clear off Derbent (the deep Derbent depression holds about 15 m Secchi in January); grey-brown near the Terek, Sulak and Samur mouths; the west coast is always less clear than the east.
optics.turbidityCause: River plumes (Terek, Sulak, Samur) and the southward coastal current; plankton

salinityPsu.note: Middle Caspian surface about 12-13, lower near the river mouths (ru.wikipedia). Nearshore Secchi values are estimates; the 15 m and the river-mouth minima are az.wikipedia.

hazards.danger: Underwater masonry where the walls ran into the sea (estimate, from the 918 subsidence)

hazards.danger: Ice-bound shore (az.wikipedia odds)

the Caucasus foothills close behind the beach

records.change_800_to_1066: The 918 earthquake sinks part of Derbent's shore; the sea falls from about -24/-25 m toward -28 m after 977, leaving the wall ends drier (Naderi Beni et al. 2013; Barbaro in the 15th century saw the wall 'emerged'). Samandar is destroyed in 965-969.
records.then_vs_now: A sea 3-4 m higher than today's c. 800 (estimate): the walls stood in the water; today their seaward ends are on land. No modern port at Makhachkala.

records.name: Baku bay and the Apsheron peninsula

tide.phaseNote: No tide. Wind set-up and earthquake-driven oscillations (0.45 m in 958; up to 1 m for 2-3 h in 1933) are the only quick changes (Naderi Beni et al. 2013, table 6).

waves.swellFrom: Inside Baku bay: S-SE; outside the peninsula: N-NW storms (the storm-wave centre lies 70-90 km north of Apsheron)
waves.notes: Apsheron is the windiest place on the Caspian: winds of 25 m/s and more every year, 42-44 m/s on the west side (az.wikipedia). Baku bay is sheltered from the north by the peninsula and partly closed by islands (knowledge). The 11 m wave is the Caspian's recorded maximum near Apsheron (ru.wikipedia). Bay values are estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: The west-coast current splits off Apsheron, one branch south along the west shore, one east (ru.wikipedia).
sea.seaIceOneIn: Coastal ice at Sumgait, north of the peninsula, in about 20% of winters (az.wikipedia); in Baku bay (guess) one winter in 10-20 c. 800; drift pack in extreme winters (az.wikipedia).
sea.notes: LEVEL evidence at Baku: a caravanserai built in Baku at -27.2 m in the 11th-13th centuries (Varushchenko, in Naderi Beni et al. 2013 table 4) and the Sabayil castle of 1232-1235 on an island in the bay, later under the sea and re-emerged in the 18th century (en.wikipedia Sabayil Castle; Naderi Beni table 3 dates the caravanserai to 1100-1150); in the 14th century 'many fortresses submerged in the city of Baku' (Naderi Beni table 4). So the bay's shore moved by hundreds of metres with each metre of level. c. 800 at about -25 m (estimate) the shore stood a little inland of the 11th-century line.

records.name: The south-east shore at Abaskun (the Gorgan mouth)

tide.phaseNote: No tide. Storm set-up floods the low coast up to a few km in the South Caspian (az.wikipedia).
tide.notes: A very flat coast: the 'Half-men Bay' (Nim-mardan) of the medieval geographers was shallow enough for fishermen to stand in (Naderi Beni et al. 2013).

waves.swellFrom: NW and N, much broken on the shallow shelf
waves.notes: When 16-20 m/s N-NW gales raise 3 m and more over 80% of the Middle and South Caspian, waves at the far south end stay under 2 m (az.wikipedia). Inshore values are estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Weak, wind-driven (estimate).
sea.seaIceOneIn: Never (estimate; the south freezes only rarely in extreme winters, az.wikipedia).
sea.notes: LEVEL: Abaskun was a port from the start of the 9th century to the 13th and lay on the shoreline while the sea stood about -24 m; it is put at about -24 m elevation near today's Gomishan, was 'the best port of the Caspian' to Istakhri, with foul air and mosquitoes (marsh and lagoons) to Ibn Hawqal, raided by the Rus between 880 and 913 (al-Mas'udi), and drowned in the 13th-14th-century rise to -19 m (Naderi Beni et al. 2013). The Gorgan's present delta mouth dates only from 1854 (same). Gorgan Bay today is a lagoon of about 100,000 ha behind the Miankaleh spit, at most 2 m deep (en.wikipedia Gulf of Gorgan); with the sea at about -24/-25 m c. 800 the lagoon and coast were laid out differently (Naderi Beni et al.: the Nim-mardan bay was more likely today's Hassanqoli bay).

optics.colour: Cloudy greenish-tan over the shallow sand and silt shelf; brown at the river mouth; blue-green further out.
optics.turbidityCause: Shallow stirred silt and the Gorgan river; minimal transparency (2.5 m) along the south-east shelf from Iran to Turkmenbashi (az.wikipedia)

records.then_vs_now: The shore and Abaskun's site are now under the sea or in the lagoon zone after the 14th-century and later rises; the Gorgan mouth was elsewhere before 1854.

records.name: The Irish Sea (open water, St George's Channel to the North Channel)

tide.phaseNote: The Irish Sea's tide is one standing wave: high water is nearly simultaneous everywhere north of Wicklow (Liverpool +0.0 h, Douglas +0.4 h, Dublin +0.6 h, Workington +0.5 h vs Dover) while the south (Fishguard -3.8 h, Wexford -5.1 h) belongs to the Celtic Sea's progressive wave. Between them, off Arklow-Courtown, is a degenerate amphidrome: the range there is under 1 m (Arklow springs 0.94 m) but the streams are strong.
tide.notes: The range grows eastward: Dublin 3.85 m springs, the Isle of Man 5.0 (Port Erin) to 6.6 m (Douglas), Liverpool 8.4 m, Workington 7.5 m (computed from predictions). Streams 1-2.5 kn in the open sea, 2-3 kn off the Wicklow banks and in St George's Channel, 3-5 kn in the North Channel (knowledge: Admiralty tidal stream atlas values, not re-opened). The open sea never dries; its edges do (Liverpool Bay, the Solway, Morecambe Bay, Dundalk Bay). The given springRangeM is a mid-sea value (estimate between the shores).

waves.swellFrom: S and SSW through St George's Channel (56% of seas over 2 m at buoy M2 come from the S sector, 12% from the SW)
waves.notes: Buoy M2 (53.48 N 5.43 W, mid Irish Sea east of Dublin), 115,820 hourly values 2008-2026: Hs mean 1.17 m, median 1.00, 90% 2.19, 99% 3.59, 99.9% 4.84, max 6.64 m (16 Oct 2017, ex-hurricane Ophelia); largest single wave (Hmax) 10.2 m (28 Oct 2025); mean zero-crossing period 4.2 s, Tp mean 5.6 s, Tp 90% 8.3 s. Monthly mean Hs: Jan 1.62, Feb 1.48, Mar 1.22, Apr 0.98, May 0.84, Jun 0.81, Jul 0.75, Aug 0.84, Sep 1.06, Oct 1.35, Nov 1.52, Dec 1.67 m. A short steep fetch-limited sea: storm waves about half the Atlantic's height but at 5-8 s, close together; wind against tide over the banks steepens them further. Decision 4 (full real height) is easy to honour here.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: A weak northward residual, a few km a day (knowledge): water leaves through the North Channel; soluble Sellafield discharge reaches the North Channel in about six months to a year (verified, Wikipedia). Wind drift (about 3% of the wind) dominates what a ship feels.
sea.notes: A western channel 80-275 m deep and 30-50 km wide, shallow eastern bays under 50 m (verified, Wikipedia); Beaufort's Dyke in the North Channel 312 m (verified). Sandbanks: Bahama and King William Banks east and north of Man; Kish, Codling, Arklow and Blackwater Banks off Ireland (verified).

optics.colour: grey-green, bottle-green in sun, brown-green within 5-10 km of the English and Welsh coasts
optics.turbidityCause: tidal stirring of fine sediment over the shallow eastern half; spring plankton bloom; river plumes on the east side

salinityPsu.note: about 34-34.5 in the western channel, 32-33 in Liverpool Bay under the river plumes (knowledge). Buoy M2's salinity sensor reads 29.5-31.8 and is not trusted.

long low swell from the SSW entering St George's Channel ahead of Atlantic lows
tide lines and foam streaks along the banks
sea fog in spring and early summer when warm SW air crosses water at 9-11 C (knowledge)
Noctiluca bioluminescence on late-summer calm nights (knowledge)
glassy calms under summer highs with cat's paws crossing them

records.change_800_to_1066: No measurable change to the sea. The Medieval Climate Anomaly warms the surface a few tenths of a degree after about 950 (estimate). The Norse kingdoms of Dublin, Man and the Isles make it a busy Norse sea from the 840s.
records.then_vs_now: Relative sea level about 0.3-1 m lower than today on the Irish, Welsh and English shores (estimate: late-Holocene rise plus the modern 0.2 m; near zero on the rising Scottish side). No lights, buoys or dredged channels; the banks lay about where they lie now.

records.name: The Liffey estuary and Dublin's black pool (Duiblinn)
levels: Dublin and the east of Ireland

tide.phaseNote: Dublin HW +0.6 h vs Dover (about the same time as Liverpool).
tide.tidalLimit: Today the normal tidal limit is Islandbridge weir, about 4 km above the pool (verified, Wikipedia: Island Bridge of 1577 'at the upper tidal extremities'). c. 800: about the same place, 4-5 km above the pool and 7-8 km from the open bay (estimate: the limit is set by the river's gravel bed rising, which the weir only fixed).
tide.notes: Dublin (port) predictions: springs 3.85 m, neaps 1.27 m, mean 2.74 m (computed). The Duiblinn itself was a dark tidal pool where the Poddle met the Liffey, behind today's Dublin Castle (verified). Upstream the Gaelic settlement Áth Cliath sat at the ford of hurdles near Father Mathew Bridge (verified): at low water the Liffey there was fordable. Dublin Bay below the town dried to wide sands at low water: the North Bull Island did not yet exist (it grew after the North Bull Wall of the 1820s, knowledge) and the bay was guarded by a shifting bar.

river.name: Liffey
features: the black pool at the Poddle mouth
the ford of hurdles (Áth Cliath) upstream
mudflats and saltmarsh on both banks below the pool
gravel shoals upstream of the tide
river.bed: gravel above the tide, mud and sand in the estuary
river.notes: Long-term mean 18.0 m3/s; August monthly mean 3.7, December 29.8 (verified, Wikipedia). Today about 60% of the flow is abstracted and three ESB dams (Poulaphouca, Golden Falls, Leixlip) regulate it (verified); c. 800 the natural river was flashier: higher winter floods, lower late-summer flow. The flood figure is a guess (natural 1-in-10-year flood of a 1,256 km2 Wicklow catchment, scaled from the December 1801 flood that took the old bridge, verified only as an event). Width at the pool: c. 800 the tidal Liffey between soft banks was perhaps 100-150 m at high water, wider over the flats below; the Wood Quay excavations show the Viking-age bank stood well inland of today's quay walls, which have narrowed it to about 40-50 m (estimate from knowledge of the excavations). Gradient: Wicklow source at 500 m (verified) falling to the sea over 132 km; the lowest reach under 0.5 m/km (estimate). Ice: the river iced in the great frosts (822, 856, 917, 941, 945: the Annals say the 'rivers of Ireland' were passable).

optics.colour: tea-brown peaty water from the Wicklow bogs over a grey-brown mud bottom; the black pool really looks black
optics.turbidityCause: peat-stained (humic) water from the Liffey Head Bog and the Poddle, plus mud stirred by the tide

salinityPsu.note: brackish at the pool, fresh at low water and in floods, up to 25-30 at spring high water (estimate)

hazards.name: Dublin bar
hazards.where: the mouth of the Liffey in Dublin Bay
hazards.danger: shifting sand bar; at low water the channel over it is shallow and breaks in easterly gales (knowledge, the bar was a hazard until the 19th-century walls)

hazards.name: The drying sands of Dublin Bay
hazards.danger: a ship that misses the channel grounds and lies on the sand for half a tide

phenomena: the pool's dark mirror at slack high water
flood tide reversing the brown river at the pool
mudflats with waders at low water
peat-foam lines on the ebb
mist on the river on still autumn mornings
smoke of the longphort hanging over the water
records.change_800_to_1066: 841: the Norse naval camp (longphort) at Duiblinn (verified, Annals of Ulster 841.4); 837: sixty ships on the Liffey (AU 837.3). From the 10th century the town grows along the south bank and starts building out wattle and post-and-plank river frontages and banks (Wood Quay), narrowing the river a little at a time (knowledge).
records.then_vs_now: Then: a soft-banked tidal river with mudflats and saltmarsh, a pool at the Poddle, a ford upstream, a bay of open sands. Now: granite quay walls, a dredged port channel, the Bull Walls and North Bull Island, a weir at Islandbridge, dams upstream, 60% of the water abstracted.

records.name: Linn Duachaill: the Glyde and Dee mouth in Dundalk Bay (Annagassan)
levels: Dublin and the east of Ireland

tide.phaseNote: HW about +0.3 h vs Dover (between Drogheda +0.4 h and Kilkeel +0.2 h).
tide.tidalLimit: about 2-3 km up the Glyde and Dee above the confluence at Annagassan (estimate: low coastal plain)
tide.notes: Drogheda (4.61 m springs, 1.72 neaps) and Kilkeel (4.68 / 1.76) bracket it (computed; both are model stations). Dundalk Bay is shallow, sandy and intertidal, over 4,000 ha exposed at low tide (verified, Wikipedia). The Annals record the tide's danger here: in 1045 the king of Brega met Muirchertach ua Néill's force at Casán Linne (the Annagassan estuary) and 'the sea was in full tide against him, and Muirchertach and many others fell there' (verified, AU 1045.4): an army caught by the flood on the sands.

records.change_800_to_1066: 841: a Norse naval camp at Linn Duachaill (AU 841.4), raiding as far as Clonmacnoise (AU 842.6); abbot of Linn Duachaill killed 842; 926-927 a fleet under Alpthann landed there and wintered (AU 926.5, 927.3). The camp is not mentioned after 930.
records.then_vs_now: Little changed physically: no harbour works beyond a small quay; the Glyde and Dee were drained and embanked upstream in the 19th-20th centuries (knowledge), so floods then spread wider over the low fields.

records.name: Peel: the Neb mouth and St Patrick's Isle (Holmr)

tide.phaseNote: Port Erin HW +0.2 h vs Dover; Peel about the same (estimate).
tide.tidalLimit: the Neb is tidal a few hundred metres above its mouth (estimate)
tide.notes: Port Erin, 15 km down the same west coast, stands in: springs 4.96 m, neaps 1.92, mean 3.74 m (computed). The Neb harbour dries at low water: a floodgate was installed only in 2005 so boats could float at low tide (verified). Norse ships lay in the Neb's mouth sheltered by St Patrick's Isle (verified: 'used the harbour on the River Neb as a shelter for their longships'). St Patrick's Isle is a tidal island (verified); c. 800 it was reached across the Neb mouth on foot at low water (estimate; the causeway is modern).

river.name: Neb
river.notes: Small upland stream from 320 m (verified source height); discharge is a guess for a catchment of about 70 km2 at 0.02 m3/s/km2.

waves.notes: estimate from buoy M2 (mid Irish Sea, west of Man, Hs mean 1.17, 99% 3.59): Peel faces the open sea to the west; the bay is sheltered from the east. A westerly gale makes the bay unusable.

records.name: The Dee estuary and the tidal Dee to Chester (Legacæstir)

tide.phaseNote: At the mouth (Hilbre) HW about Dover +0.0 h like Liverpool; at Chester about 1-1.5 h later, with a short flood and a long ebb (estimate, typical of a shallow funnel estuary).
tide.tidalLimit: Today: Chester weir, built for Hugh Lupus's mills (late 11th c., after 1070; verified that he built it), which spring tides overtop. c. 800: no weir; the tide ran on above Chester, probably to about Aldford-Farndon, roughly 10-15 km above the city and 40-45 km from Hilbre (guess: the Dee's gradient above Chester is gentle and the natural rock bar under the weir was the only check).

bore.name: Dee bore
bore.when: big spring tides, 1-3 days after new and full moon, in the canalised channel above Connah's Quay (today); c. 800 it would have run in the natural channel towards Chester

tide.notes: Mouth: the Wirral side (Formby/Flint model stations) springs 8.3 m, neaps 2.8 m (computed); Liverpool 8.41/3.23. At Chester the river bed cuts off the lower tide, so the range felt there is only the top part: springs perhaps 3-4.5 m, neaps under 1 m or nothing (estimate). The bore exists and has been studied (Simpson et al. 2004, cited in Wikipedia 'Tidal bore'); its height is a guess. Ships lay to in the Dee waiting for wind and tide (14th c., verified).

river.name: Dee (Afon Dyfrdwy)
features: Roman and early medieval harbour by the walls (the Roodee, already silting)
red sandstone bluff under the city walls
wide tidal sands and saltmarsh below Chester
rock bar at the later weir site
river.bed: sand and mud; sandstone bar at Chester
river.notes: NRFA 67033 Dee at Chester Suspension Bridge (1994-2025): mean 33.5 m3/s, Q95 4.98, Q10 88.9, max daily 306.6. NRFA 67015 Manley Hall (1937-2025): mean 31.4, max 521 (14 Dec 1964), QMED 229. Today Llyn Tegid (Bala Lake) and upland reservoirs regulate it (knowledge); c. 800 the natural river had sharper floods and lower summer flows. The Roodee was Chester's Roman harbour until the river silted, helped by the weir (verified); the 1732-36 New Cut moved the river to the Welsh side and failed to stop silting (verified). So c. 800 the channel to Chester was deeper and nearer the Wirral bank than now, and ships of the period could reach the city on the tide (estimate).

optics.colour: grey-brown, milky with fine mud; the river above Chester browner and clearer
optics.turbidityCause: tidal resuspension of estuary mud and fine sand

salinityPsu.note: fresh at Chester at low water, brackish at high water springs, 30+ at Hilbre (estimate)

hazards.name: The Dee sands
hazards.where: the whole outer estuary, Hilbre to Flint
hazards.danger: the estuary is several miles wide (verified) and mostly dry at low water; the channels shift; a ship off the channel lies on the sand

hazards.name: The flood tide over the sands
hazards.danger: the tide comes over the flats faster than a man walks (knowledge)

phenomena: the bore's small wave running up the channel on big springs
sandstone walls and the red bluff mirrored at high water
skeins of geese over the saltmarsh
mist on the river at dawn
the whole estuary turning to shining sand at low water
records.change_800_to_1066: 907: Æthelflæd refounds Chester as a burh; 10th century Chester is a major mint and port for the Irish Sea trade (knowledge). 973: King Edgar rowed on the Dee at Chester by subject kings (knowledge, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and John of Worcester). Silting continues; the weir (after 1070) will make it worse. The estuary is still navigable to the city through the period.
records.then_vs_now: Then: a natural tidal river to and above Chester, no weir, no New Cut, a deeper channel on the English side, wide open sands. Now: canalised 1737 to the Welsh side, weir at Chester, the upper estuary silted into saltmarsh and dry land, Chester a river town with no port.

Dee Estuary (several miles wide, silting, Wirral harbours, 1737 cut)

records.name: Meols and Hoyle Lake: the north Wirral shore between the Dee and the Mersey

tide.phaseNote: Liverpool Gladstone Dock HW +0.0 h vs Dover (computed); Meols the same within minutes.
tide.notes: Liverpool Gladstone Dock stands in: springs 8.41 m, neaps 3.23 m, mean 6.23 m (computed); highest predicted HW 9.68 m above chart datum. This is the largest tide of the Irish Sea outside the Solway and Morecambe Bay: at low springs the shore uncovers for kilometres. Hoyle Lake, the channel between Hilbre Island and Dove Point, sheltered by Hoyle Bank with about 20 ft (6 m) of water, was a safe anchorage for ships too large for the Dee (verified, 17th-18th c. description; c. 800 its depth is unknown). records.change_800_to_1066: Meols was a beach market and landing for some 2,400 years with finds through the Viking period (verified); Norse settlement of the Wirral after 902 (knowledge). The shore was eroding slowly.
records.then_vs_now: Then the north Wirral shore stood further seaward: 19th-century erosion (made worse by dredging for Liverpool) washed the medieval site's finds out of the shore, and an 1890s sea wall followed (verified). How far seaward is unknown; a guess of 200-500 m (the finds came from a now-vanished land surface). Hoyle Lake was open water then; it has since silted (knowledge).

records.name: The Menai Strait and the Swellies

tide.phaseNote: Caernarfon HW -0.3 h vs Dover, Bangor -0.2 h (computed; the model stations show only a small lag). records.name: The Clyde estuary at Dumbarton Rock (Alt Clut)

tide.phaseNote: Greenock HW +1.4 h vs Dover (computed); Dumbarton about 15-20 min later (estimate).
tide.tidalLimit: Today the tidal weir at Glasgow Green (verified), about 25 km above Dumbarton. c. 800: about the same reach, near Glasgow, where shoals and fords stopped it (estimate); but the tide reaching Glasgow was much smaller than today's, because the dredged channel now lets more of it through (knowledge: the range at Glasgow grew several-fold after 18th-19th-century deepening).

The pre-dredging Clyde was shallow above Dumbarton: shoals and shallows let only small vessels up (verified); fords at Dumbuck below Dumbarton and further up with only a foot or two at low water in the 18th century (knowledge, Smeaton's 1755 survey).

records.change_800_to_1066: Raids from the 820s; a longphort near Waterford in 853 (verified); Woodstown's large 9th-century Norse site (about 4,000 objects, verified) occupied c. 840-940; refounded at Waterford in 914 by Ottir and Ragnall (verified) and built into a town.
records.then_vs_now: Then: no quay wall (the mile-long Quay is post-medieval), no bridges, wooded banks, natural floods over the low callows of the Suir above Waterford. Now: quays, a port at Belview, flood defences.

records.name: Cork Harbour and the Lee marshes (Corcach)

tide.phaseNote: Cobh -5.2 h vs Dover (computed); Cork city about 20-30 min later (estimate).
tide.tidalLimit: Today the Lee weir in the city (verified, the river 'flows over the Lee weir' before splitting). c. 800 the tide ran a little above the marsh islands, to about the head of the marshes 1-2 km upstream of the later city (estimate).
tide.notes: Cobh springs 3.68 / neaps 1.72 m; Cork (model) 3.91 / 1.31 (computed). The harbour is 4-14 fathoms (7-26 m) deep (verified, 1835 figure); Lough Mahon (the upper harbour) is shallow and dries in part (knowledge). The Lee once ran through the city area 'as a maze of channels' (verified); Corcach means marsh.

river.name: Lee
features: the great harbour's islands (Great Island, Haulbowline, Spike)
river.notes: Mean 40.4 m3/s, catchment 1,253.5 km2 (verified, Wikipedia). Today two ESB dams (Inniscarra, Carrigadrohid, 1950s) regulate it; in the 2009 flood a release of 535 m3/s added to an already flooded river (verified). c. 800 natural floods spread across the marsh islands every winter; the flood value is a guess on that order.

herons and egrets on the mud
wooded hills round a landlocked sea
records.change_800_to_1066: St Finbarr's monastery at Corcach; Viking raids from the 820s (Corcach burned 839, AU 839.10); Norse town on the marsh island from about 915 (levels data).
records.then_vs_now: Then: a braid of channels through marsh islands; no quays, no weir, no dams; a wider upper harbour with fringing saltmarsh. Now: the city built over the islands with two channels, dams upstream, a port at Ringaskiddy.

records.name: The Shannon estuary from Loop Head to Limerick (Hlymrekr)

tide.phaseNote: Tarbert -5.1 h vs Dover (computed); Limerick about 1-1.5 h later than the mouth (estimate: 100 km of estuary).
tide.tidalLimit: Today the tide runs past Limerick to the foot of Ardnacrusha's tailrace (verified). c. 800 (before the 1929 scheme) the natural limit was at Limerick itself, where the river came down over the rapids by King's Island (the Curragower falls, knowledge); about 100 km from Loop Head (the estuary is 102.1 km, verified).

bore.name: Shannon bore
bore.when: occasional, on big spring tides in the upper estuary (verified that it occurs, e.g. 21 Sep 2013; height and speed are guesses)

tide.notes: Range up to about 5.44 m at Limerick docks (verified, Wikipedia). Tarbert (verified station) springs 4.38 / neaps 1.98 m; the model station 'Shannon' 4.61 / 1.29 (computed): the range grows up the estuary towards Limerick. Streams 3-4 kn at springs in the narrows between Tarbert and Kilcredaun (knowledge); the estuary's tidal power was assessed at 111-367 GWh a year (verified), a measure of how hard it runs. The Fergus estuary to the north is a great expanse of mud (knowledge).

river.name: Shannon (tidal reach)
features: King's Island between the Shannon and the Abbey River
river.bed: mud and sand; rock at Limerick
river.notes: Long-term mean 208.1 m3/s at Limerick (verified); at Athlone 98 m3/s (verified); the whole estuary takes about 300 m3/s with the Fergus, Maigue and Deel (verified). In wet periods more than 400 m3/s leaves Lough Derg (verified); the flood value at Limerick is a guess with the tributaries. The low value is a guess (Lough Derg and Lough Ree buffer the dry season).

optics.colour: brown, mud-laden in the upper estuary; green-grey at the mouth
optics.turbidityCause: tidal mud; the river's peat-brown water

salinityPsu.note: estimate at Limerick on the flood; fresh on the ebb; 34 at Loop Head

hazards.name: Mud and shoals of the upper estuary
hazards.danger: grounding at low water; a long wait for the flood

hazards.name: Tarbert-Kilcredaun narrows
hazards.danger: 3-4 kn springs; a westerly swell against the ebb at the mouth is dangerous (knowledge)

hazards.name: Limerick rapids
hazards.danger: the river falls out of the hills here; no sail past it

phenomena: the tide flooding brown up a 100 km estuary
dolphins in the lower estuary (knowledge: a resident bottlenose population)
mud banks gleaming at low water
the roar of the rapids above Limerick in flood
records.change_800_to_1066: 812: Vikings sail up the Shannon to Limerick and burn Mungret (verified); 845 'the ships of Luimnech' (AU 845.1); Norse town on King's Island from 922 (levels; AU 922.3 'the fleet of Luimnech ... went on Loch Rí'); 937 the Limerick Norse fight the Dublin Norse on Lough Ree (verified).
records.then_vs_now: Then: the tide stopped at the rapids of Limerick and the whole Shannon above came down through rapids and falls. Now: Ardnacrusha (1929) takes most of the water through a headrace and tailrace; the old channel past Castleconnell gets a legal minimum of 10 m3/s (verified) and the tide runs up to the tailrace.

records.name: The Shannon between Killaloe and Limerick: the Falls of Doonass and Castleconnell rapids

tide.tidalLimit: the tide ends at Limerick, the foot of this reach (estimate, see shannon_estuary_limerick)

river.name: Shannon (Killaloe to Limerick)
features: the Falls of Doonass, the largest fall on the river (verified)
river.notes: The river falls 30 m in 20 km here (verified): 1.5 m/km, against 18 m in its first 250 km. This reach was the barrier to sailing: ships must be rowed, poled and hauled up the rapids at moderate flow, or carried/dragged round the falls (estimate; the Annals show Limerick fleets reaching Lough Derg and Lough Ree, so they passed it, AU 922.3). Discharge: the outflow of Lough Derg, a little less than at Limerick (estimate); >400 m3/s in wet periods (verified). Flow speeds are estimates for a 1.5 m/km rocky reach. Ice: a rapid this steep does not freeze over.

optics.colour: dark amber-brown water turning white over the rocks
optics.turbidityCause: humic colour from the midland bogs; air in the rapids

hazards.name: Falls of Doonass
hazards.danger: a true fall; boats are carried or hauled round

hazards.name: Castleconnell rapids
hazards.danger: standing waves and rocks; in flood unrunnable

phenomena: standing waves and white water
spray rising off the falls in flood
salmon leaping the falls in summer
the roar heard from a distance
records.change_800_to_1066: No physical change. The Dál gCais (later Brian Bórama's dynasty) rule the Killaloe end at Kincora from the 10th century (knowledge).
records.then_vs_now: Then the whole Shannon came down this way: Doonass in full roar. Now Ardnacrusha's headrace takes nearly all of it and the old channel gets 10 m3/s (verified): the falls are 'temporarily restored to their former glory' only when more than 400 m3/s spills (verified). Lateral canals and locks (Plassey-Errina, 18th c.) were added for navigation (verified).

records.name: Lough Derg (Loch Deirgdheirc) on the Shannon

river.name: Shannon (Lough Derg)

river.notes: Up to 36 m deep, 130 km2 (verified); navigable for its full length (verified). Flows are those passing through (estimates, see the rapids record). Winter levels about 1 m above summer (estimate). Ice: the Annals' great frosts (822, 856, 917, 941, 945) made 'the principal lakes' passable on foot; c. 800 a full freeze about once in 40 years (estimate from those entries), shore ice most winters.

records.then_vs_now: Then: natural level, falling in summer. Now: held up for Ardnacrusha (verified: the scheme envisaged altering upper lake levels for storage), so the natural summer drop and the winter flood rise were larger then (estimate).

records.name: The middle Shannon and its callows at Clonmacnoise (Cluain moccu Nóis)

river.name: Shannon (Athlone to Portumna)
features: the callows: flood meadows up to 1-2 km wide that drown each winter
eskers (the Eiscir Riada) meeting the river at Clonmacnoise (knowledge)
river.notes: At Athlone, 15 km upstream, the mean is 98 m3/s (verified); Clonmacnoise adds the Suck lower down, so the given values are for the reach above it. The Shannon falls only 18 m in its first 250 km (verified): about 0.07 m/km, flatter still on the callows (estimate 0.03-0.05). Hence a slow, deep-looking river whose low, shallow grade floods the callows (verified); the flood rise and spread are estimates. Low and flood flows are guesses (the lakes buffer them). 'Callow' is from Irish caladh, flood-meadow (verified). Ice: the frost years in the Annals; the river's slowness lets it freeze far more readily than a fast river.

optics.colour: dark tea-brown, black in the deep water, amber over gravel; silver sheets of floodwater over the callows in winter
optics.turbidityCause: humic staining from the midland raised bogs

hazards.danger: the channel vanishes under a lake in winter; a ship can stray onto drowned meadow

corncrakes calling from the summer meadows (verified species)
whooper swans and geese on the winter floods
river mist each autumn dawn
the monastery's round towers reflected in still water
records.change_800_to_1066: Clonmacnoise was attacked repeatedly: by the Irish at least 27 times, the Vikings at least 7, the Normans 6 (verified); raided from Linn Duachaill 842 (AU 842.6), burned by Turgéis's men from Lough Ree 845 (AU 845.3), plundered by the Limerick fleet from Lough Ree 922 (AU 922.3). The river itself unchanged; after 950 the MCA dries summers a little (estimate).
records.then_vs_now: Then: no weirs, locks or lateral canals (Thomas Omer's works from 1755, verified), no dredging; summer lows lower and natural; floods spread unchecked. Now: the navigation is held at levels by weirs (Athlone, Meelick), and the early summer floods that 'became predominant' drove the corncrake out (verified).

records.name: The Severn sea: the Bristol Channel and the Severn estuary

tide.phaseNote: Ilfracombe about -4.5 h, Avonmouth -3.9 h, Beachley -3.8 h vs Dover (computed): the tide runs in from the Celtic Sea and climbs as the channel narrows.
tide.tidalLimit: Today the Severn is tidal to Gloucester's weirs (Maisemore, Llanthony, 19th c.), with big springs overtopping Tewkesbury weir and lifting the level at Worcester a foot (verified). c. 800: no weirs: the tide ran naturally to about Tewkesbury, some 30 km above Gloucester and roughly 110 km above Avonmouth (estimate).

bore.name: Severn bore
bore.when: about 130 days a year, two a day, 1-3 days after new and full moon; the largest between 9 and 11 in the morning and evening (GMT); largest recorded 2.8 m on 15 Oct 1966; made bigger by strong SW-W wind, low pressure and low river (verified). Starts above Sharpness (knowledge) and runs to Gloucester at 13-21 km/h (7-11 kn, verified)

tide.notes: Avonmouth springs 12.08 m, neaps 4.81 m, mean 9.20 m (computed); highest predicted HW 13.38 m above datum. Beachley/Aust 12.36 / 4.13, Cardiff 11.62 / 4.07, Minehead 9.80, Ilfracombe 8.55 (computed). Wikipedia gives about 13 m and calls it second only to the Bay of Fundy (verified); 'about 15 m' on the estuary page is the extreme. Streams: 5-8 kn in the Shoots and off Aust at springs, 2-4 kn in the outer channel (knowledge). At low tide large parts of the channel are mudflats (verified).

river.name: Severn (with the Wye and Usk entering the estuary)
features: the Shoots and the English Stones (rock channel under today's crossings, knowledge)
river.notes: NRFA 54057 Severn at Haw Bridge: mean 113.8 m3/s, Q95 21.2, Q10 282, max 1,340 (the max may carry tidal backwater). Into the estuary also come the Wye (55023 Redbrook: 73.7) and the Usk (56001 Chainbridge: 28.9). Estuary width 3.2 km at Aust, 14 km Cardiff-Weston (verified); the 3000 m is a mid value for the inner estuary. Most of the estuary and embayments under 30 ft (9 m), an east-west valley 65-100 ft deep in the channel (verified).

waves.swellFrom: W Atlantic swell up the channel, dying inward
waves.notes: estimate: the outer channel gets Celtic Sea swell (surf on the west-facing beaches, verified); the inner estuary only a short steep chop, worst with wind against a 5-8 kn stream

sea.notes: The 1607 flood (30 January) drowned thousands along the channel; storm and tide, or a tsunami, are both argued (verified).

optics.colour: opaque chocolate-brown in the estuary, coffee-and-milk; greener and clearer only west of Minehead and Barry
optics.turbidityCause: one of the most turbid estuaries in Europe: the huge tide keeps fine mud in suspension (knowledge: grams per litre near the bed)

salinityPsu.note: estimate: about 30 at the channel's mouth, fresh above Sharpness at low water

hazards.name: The Severn bore
hazards.where: above Sharpness to Gloucester (and c. 800 beyond)
hazards.danger: a 1-2.8 m breaking wave and a sudden reversal of the stream: capsizes boats moored or anchored in the channel

hazards.name: The Shoots and English Stones
hazards.where: the narrows off Aust and Beachley
hazards.danger: 5-8 kn streams over rock ledges (knowledge)

hazards.name: Mud and sand banks
hazards.danger: kilometres of mud at low water; the 12 m tide floods them fast

phenomena: the bore, a brown rolling wave with a rumble, followed by a surge of whelps
the estuary emptying to a world of shining mud and channels
water too brown to see a hand in
huge skies and low light on the levels
Flat Holm and Steep Holm as landmarks
records.change_800_to_1066: The bore was known: William of Malmesbury describes it at Gloucester about 1125 (knowledge, not re-opened). The levels (Gwent, Somerset) were being re-embanked from the post-Roman wetland in the 10th-13th centuries (knowledge: Rippon, The Severn Estuary, 1997).
records.then_vs_now: Then: after the post-Roman flooding, much of the Gwent and Somerset levels was tidal saltmarsh, so the estuary's intertidal area was larger and the tide spread wider (knowledge, estimate of extent). No weirs on the river, no docks at Avonmouth or Cardiff, no Gloucester and Sharpness canal (1827, verified), no crossings.

records.name: The tidal Avon through its gorge to Bristol (Brycgstow)

tide.phaseNote: about -3.6 h vs Dover (Avonmouth -3.9 h plus about 20 min for 12 km of river, estimate)
tide.tidalLimit: Today the tidal Avon runs to Netham weir (1809), with the old course as the impounded harbour (verified). c. 800 the tide ran on above Bristol to about Hanham-Keynsham, roughly 8-10 km above the town and about 20-25 km from the Severn (estimate).

bore.name: Avon tidal surge
bore.when: big springs only; a small undular front (guess)

tide.notes: At Avonmouth the spring range is 12.1 m (computed). Up the river the low water is cut off by the bed: the river 'dries to a steep-sided muddy channel at low tide' (verified), so at Bristol the range felt is the upper part, about 9-10 m at springs (estimate). Within the gorge the level swings about 47 ft (14 m) at the largest tides (verified, Bristol Harbour article). Ships of the period lay aground on the mud at low water in the town reach (verified for the pre-1809 harbour).

river.name: Avon (Bristol)
features: the Avon Gorge: 2.4 km long, over 700 ft (213 m) wide and 300 ft (91 m) deep at the suspension bridge site (verified)
tight meanders below the town (Horseshoe Bend, knowledge)
the Frome confluence at the town
river.notes: NRFA 53018 Avon at Bathford (1969-2025): mean 20.1 m3/s, Q95 2.64, Q10 50.4, max 249.9; 53003 Bath St James mean 20.5 (verified). The width given is the low-water channel at Bristol (estimate); at high water springs the river fills to perhaps 80-100 m between steep mud banks 8 m high (estimate). The Frome was diverted into St Augustine's Reach in the 1240s (verified): in 1000 it still met the Avon in its natural course by the bridge.

optics.colour: Severn brown; grey-brown glistening mud at low water
optics.turbidityCause: Severn mud carried in by the tide

salinityPsu.note: estimate: brackish at high water, fresh at low

hazards.name: Grounding in the gorge
hazards.danger: a ship caught by the ebb in the gorge falls 8-10 m onto mud and rock and may break her back

hazards.name: Tidal timing
hazards.danger: the passage must be made on one flood; the stream runs 3-4 kn (estimate)

phenomena: water rising 9-10 m up the gorge walls in a few hours
steep glistening mud banks at low water
the river emptying to a stream at the bottom of a muddy trench
limestone cliffs and woods of the gorge
records.change_800_to_1066: Bristol (Brycgstow, the place at the bridge) grows into a town about 1000-1050 (levels: from 1010); trade with Dublin and Ireland follows (knowledge). No physical change.
records.then_vs_now: Then: a fully tidal river through the town, ships aground at low water, the Frome in its own bed. Now: the Floating Harbour (1809) holds the old river at high water; the tidal Avon goes round by the New Cut (verified).

records.name: The Camel estuary and the Doom Bar (Lanwethinoc, Padstow)

tide.phaseNote: about -5.7 h vs Dover (Wadebridge model station, computed)

tide.notes: Newquay (springs 6.78, neaps 2.01) and the Wadebridge model station (7.17 / 2.13) (computed). The Doom Bar is a sand bar across the mouth, more than 60% shell sand, that restricts access (verified); in storms ships risked wreck on the coast rather than the channel (1859 testimony, verified); the bar was called 'Dunbar sands' and 'the Doom-bar' by 1761 (verified).

golden sand banks at low water

records.then_vs_now: Then the bar and channel were natural and the main channel lay near the western cliffs (it moved away from them early in the 20th century, verified). Since then millions of tons of sand have been dredged and carried off for lime (verified: 100,000 tons a year in 1839; 120,000 in 2009); the bar was larger then (estimate).

records.name: The western Mediterranean (open sea of O15: Alboran, Balearic and Ligurian seas)

tide.phaseNote: The Atlantic tide leaks in through Gibraltar and dies eastward: about 0.6 m at springs at Malaga, 0.1-0.2 m at Marseille (tide tables, Oct 2026). The open-basin values are an average (estimate).
tide.notes: Practically tideless for a ship: wind set-up and air pressure (1 cm per hPa) move the level more than the tide does. Render the tide as a 0.1-0.3 m breathing at the shore only.

waves.notes: Record Hs 8.44 m off Valencia in Storm Gloria (20 Jan 2020); previous record 8.15 m near Mahon (Jan 2003); single wave 14.2 m at Dragonera (Wikipedia, Storm Gloria). Mean and Hs99 are estimates for the open Balearic-Provencal basin. The Mediterranean sea is short and steep for its height: Tp 5-8 s against 8-12 s on the Atlantic, so a 4 m sea here is harder on a small ship than a 4 m Atlantic swell (estimate from fetch-limited growth, weather_and_sea_state.md 1.3).

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Atlantic water enters at Gibraltar as a jet, turns through the Alboran gyres and runs east along Africa as the Algerian Current (0.3-0.5 m/s, with eddies 50-100 km across); the Northern (Liguro-Provencal-Catalan) Current runs SW along Italy, France and Spain at 0.2-0.5 m/s (knowledge, values estimate). A sailing ship feels 0.5-1 knot of set.
sea.notes: Winds make this sea. Mistral (Rhone valley, N-NW) and tramontane (Languedoc, NW) average about 50 km/h and reach 100 km/h, last from 1 day to over a week, are commonest in winter and spring, and clear the sky within two hours (Wikipedia, Mistral); they blow offshore from the Gulf of Lion toward the Balearics, so the danger is being blown out to sea, not onto the coast. Medicanes (tropical-like lows) form about 0.75 a year in the western basin, autumn to January, winds to 144 km/h (Wikipedia, Medicane). Winter mistral drives deep convection in the Gulf of Lion (cold, salty water sinks).

optics.colour: Deep ultramarine to cobalt blue offshore (one of the clearest seas in the world); greener and paler on the Gulf of Lion shelf after spring blooms and in the Rhone plume
optics.turbidityCause: Plankton only offshore (oligotrophic); river silt only in plumes off the Rhone and Ebro

salinityPsu.note: About 36.5 in the Atlantic jet of the Alboran, rising to 38 in the Balearic and Ligurian seas (knowledge, estimate); fresher (35-37) in the Rhone and Ebro plumes

hazards.name: Isla de Alboran and its shoals
hazards.danger: Low rock far from land, hard to see at night (estimate)

hazards.name: Columbretes
hazards.danger: Volcanic islets 50 km offshore on the Ebro-Valencia route (knowledge)

phenomena: Mistral days: hard blue sky, white horses to the horizon, blown spray, long visibility (mountains seen 150 km away, Wikipedia Mistral), a cold short sea
Glassy summer calms (July-August) with a heat haze and a long low swell from a distant storm; cat's paws in the afternoon sea breeze
A seasonal thermocline in summer: very clear warm surface water over cold depths
Bioluminescence (Noctiluca and dinoflagellates) on calm late-spring and summer nights near the coasts (estimate)
Medicane: a small spiral storm with an eye, autumn-winter, rare (about one every year or two in the western basin)
Tuna shoals boiling at the surface in spring off the Strait and the Balearics; dolphins in the Alboran
records.change_800_to_1066: The open sea itself barely changed. Relative sea level stood about 0.3-0.5 m below today on stable coasts (knowledge, estimate). After about 950 the Medieval Climate Anomaly warmed the surface perhaps 0.5 C (guess); in 793 the decision-17 offset (-0.8 C) applies. Saracen fleets from al-Andalus and Ifriqiya, later the Fatimids, make the open sea a raiding sea; the sea state is the same.
records.then_vs_now: No man-made change to the open water apart from modern pollution and plastics (leave out). Colour and clarity c. 800 as now or slightly clearer (no modern nutrient load, estimate).

records.name: The Strait of Gibraltar (al-Jazira al-Khadra' and Sabta)

tide.phaseNote: Atlantic semidiurnal tide, range falling from about 2-3 m at Cadiz to about 1.5 m at Tarifa and 0.8-1.0 m at Ceuta and Algeciras (Ceuta table: 0.5 m to 0.8 m approaching springs, Oct 2026; Cadiz and Tarifa values knowledge). The tidal stream reverses the surface flow near the coasts for part of each tide while the mid-strait surface keeps flowing east.
tide.notes: The mid-strait surface stream is always eastward on average (the Atlantic inflow) and strongest on the flood; at springs the surface current through the Tarifa narrows reaches 3-4 knots and over the Camarinal sill the tide drives up to about 5 knots (knowledge, estimate). Inshore counter-streams on both shores at the right state of tide are what let an oared or sailing ship work west against the inflow (knowledge).

waves.swellFrom: W (Atlantic swell rolling in with the poniente) and E (levante wind sea, short and steep)
waves.notes: Wind against current is the strait's own sea: a levante blowing west against the eastward inflow stacks a short, breaking, confused sea in the narrows (knowledge). Mean and Hs99 are estimates.

sea.nonTidalCurrent: Two-layer exchange: fresher Atlantic water flows east at the surface over a deeper, saltier Mediterranean outflow running west (Wikipedia). The surface inflow averages roughly 0.5-1 m/s (1-2 knots), about 0.8 Sverdrup (knowledge, estimate, not on the fetched pages). Internal waves: each tide, flow over the Camarinal sill (280 m) releases internal bores that run east into the Alboran; their surface signature is bands of rough, rippled water and slicks, traceable for as much as 100 km (Wikipedia, Strait of Gibraltar; Internal wave). Below the surface they reach tens of metres to about 100 m in amplitude and travel about 2 m/s (knowledge, estimate).
sea.notes: Narrowest 14.2 km, Camarinal sill 280 m, maximum depth about 900 m (Wikipedia). Two winds: levante (east) and poniente (west). The levante funnels to 20-40 knots in the strait, gale force on the western side, commonest May-October, and wears a banner cloud off the Rock about 5 km long (Wikipedia, Levant (wind)); near the Rock it reaches 40-50 knots (es.wikipedia). A ship bound west waits at Algeciras or Ceuta for the poniente to drop and the levante to come.

optics.colour: Dark Atlantic blue-green, very clear; slick bands and rip lines from the internal waves
optics.turbidityCause: Plankton; mixing over the sill brings nutrients up (knowledge)

salinityPsu.note: Atlantic surface water 36-36.5; the Mediterranean outflow below about 38 (knowledge, estimate)

records.change_800_to_1066: Physically the same through the period. Algeciras (al-Jazira al-Khadra') is the Umayyad crossing port from 711; Ceuta (Sabta) passes to Cordoba in 931 (levels_793.json from-date). Relative sea level some 0.3-0.5 m lower than now (estimate).
records.then_vs_now: No harbour moles; Algeciras is a beach harbour at the Rio de la Miel; Gibraltar is unfortified until 1160 (knowledge). The water is unchanged.

Malaga's shore lay further inland than now; the Guadalmedina's silt has pushed it out several hundred metres since (knowledge, estimate).
records.then_vs_now: No harbour moles at either port; ships beach or anchor off the shore under the Alcazaba. Malaga's medieval sea reached roughly today's Alameda (knowledge, estimate).

records.name: The lower Ebro to Turtusha (Tortosa) and its mouth

tide.phaseNote: Microtidal sea; the tide is negligible in the river (estimate).
tide.tidalLimit: No tidal flow worth rendering; the salt wedge, not the tide, marks the sea's reach: today it occupies the last 5 km at 300-400 m3/s, 18 km at 100-300 m3/s and up to 32 km below 100 m3/s (en.wikipedia, Ebro). c. 800, with a higher natural flow and a shorter delta, it rarely reached far upstream except in late-summer droughts (estimate).
tide.notes: The sea's level at the mouth follows wind set-up and pressure; Storm Gloria (2020) pushed the sea up to 3 km inland over the delta's rice fields (Wikipedia, Storm Gloria).

river.name: Ebro (Iberus; Nahr Ibruh)
river.notes: Today's mean at the mouth is 426 m3/s after the 20th century cut the flow by about 29% (en.wikipedia, Ebro), so the natural mean was about 600 m3/s (derived: 426/0.71). Floods: 23,484 m3/s at Tortosa on 23 Oct 1907 with 9.65 m on the gauge, about 20,000 in Oct 1937; drought low 32 m3/s (modern, dams) (es.wikipedia, Ebro). Flood season Oct-Mar, into May on the lower river; low water late August-early September at Tortosa (es.wikipedia). Width, depth, current, bank height and gradient are estimates for the reach below Tortosa. Ice: the lower Ebro almost never freezes; one in about 50 cold winters may bring shore ice (guess, with the 793 cooling).

optics.colour: Green-brown in summer, opaque ochre-brown in flood
optics.turbidityCause: Suspended silt and sand: before the dams the Ebro carried many million tonnes of sediment a year; the load fell by more than 99% in the 20th century (en.wikipedia, Ebro). c. 800 lower than its 14th-15th-century peak (deforestation came later, es.wikipedia Delta del Ebro) but far higher than today (estimate).

salinityPsu.note: Fresh at Tortosa; salt wedge near the mouth (estimate)

hazards.name: The Ebro mouth bar
hazards.where: the mouth, c. 800 well upstream of today's delta tip
hazards.danger: Shallow shifting bar, breaking in easterlies; entry only in fair weather (estimate)

hazards.name: Shifting sand bars and islands
hazards.danger: Grounding at low water in late summer (estimate)

phenomena: Brown flood water carrying trees in autumn
Salt-wedge slick line where clear sea water slides under the brown river
Reed beds and lagoons on the young delta
Mosquito-thick summer air (malaria country, knowledge)
records.change_800_to_1066: The delta was small c. 800: one view has an estuary reaching toward Tortosa in Roman times, the other a modest delta already (es.wikipedia, Delta del Ebro); Amposta was a seaport in the 4th century and is now well inland (en.wikipedia, Ebro). The big growth came in the 14th-15th centuries with deforestation, so through 793-1066 the coast stays far closer to Tortosa than today, perhaps 10-20 km (guess). Tortosa is the Umayyad frontier port and shipyard; besieged by the Franks 804-811 (knowledge).
records.then_vs_now: No dams (Mequinenza, Ribarroja, Flix), no irrigation draw: more water, far more sediment, a bigger seasonal swing. No modern delta of 320 km2 (es.wikipedia): the 800 mouth is a smaller lobe much further inland.

Lagoons are deeper and more open to the sea than now (the etang de Bages-Sigean was an open gulf in antiquity, fr.wikipedia). records.then_vs_now: No dykes (they begin in the Middle Ages, fr.wikipedia Camargue), no salt-works on the modern scale, no Sete, no Port-la-Nouvelle harbour, no modern seawalls. The coast moves with every storm.

In the Middle Ages the Aude split: one branch south through Narbonne to the sea by La Clape, another east to the lagoons; a great flood in 1320 swept the dam away and the river left Narbonne (en.wikipedia, Narbonne). records.name: The lower Rhone to Arelate (Arles)
levels: The Gulf of Lion and Provence

tide.phaseNote: The sea's 0.1-0.2 m tide does not reach Arles in any way a ship would feel (estimate).
